"Fitting a model" sounds like a single act. It is really a search. The algorithm has a
way of scoring how wrong it currently is, and a rule for changing its parameters to be
slightly less wrong, and it repeats until further changes stop helping.

Understanding that loop is worth an hour of your time, because it explains a great
deal that otherwise looks arbitrary: why models need scaled inputs, why fits
sometimes fail to converge, why two runs give different answers, and what a
regularisation penalty is actually penalising.

It also connects to ground you may already stand on. Least-squares regression and
maximum likelihood are not a separate world from machine learning: they are the same
machinery with a different scorecard.

This section settles three debts. Section 2 asked you to [scale your
predictors](../02-marine-data/scaling-and-encoding.qmd) without giving the real reason;
[gradient descent](gradient-descent.qmd) supplies it, and it is worth a factor of about
ninety in computing. [Section
3](../03-supervised-learning/linear-and-polynomial-regression.qmd) showed a linear model
predicting negative fish; [maximum likelihood](maximum-likelihood.qmd) explains that this
was a distributional assumption made silently, not a flaw in the method. And the
regularisation that [section 5](../05-generalisation/regularisation.qmd) is about to
introduce as a technique turns out, on the [MAP page](map-and-priors.qmd), to be a
statement of prior belief with the Bayesian label removed.

::: {.callout-note}
There is more arithmetic here than elsewhere in the course, and it is all optional depth.
If you read only two pages, read [loss functions](loss-functions.qmd), because the loss is
a scientific choice your software makes for you by default, and
[reading a fit](reading-a-fit.qmd), which is the practical one.
:::
